title: Banking and Credit
summary: A bank is an institution that accepts money from the public as deposits and gives loans. Banking means accepting deposits from the public for lending or investment. The deposits are repayable on demand or otherwise and can be withdrawn by cheque, draft or order. Money and banking go together.
(1) Accepting deposits. The bank opens an account with an account number, adds deposits, deducts withdrawals, pays interest on some deposits, and issues cheque books for withdrawals and payments.
(2) Giving loans to people who can repay later: for a TV, refrigerator, car or house, or to start a business.
(3) Keeping valuables such as jewellery and property documents in safe custody through lockers.

Credit is the claim to receive payment. When the bank lends, it becomes the lender and the borrower owes it money; this lending and borrowing creates credit. A bank keeps only a fraction of its deposits as cash, called the cash reserve ratio (CRR) and set by the banking authority. It lends the rest.

Example with CRR of 20%. A deposits ₹100. The bank keeps ₹20 and lends ₹80 to B, creating a deposit of ₹80. It keeps ₹16 of that and lends ₹64 to C, and so on. After three rounds, total deposits are 100 + 80 + 64 = ₹244.
Total credit = initial deposit × 1/CRR = 100 × 1/20% = 100 × 5 = ₹500. Of this, ₹100 is cash reserve and ₹400 is loans.

The primary deposit is the initial new deposit (₹100). Secondary deposits are created by the loans (₹80, ₹64 …). If ₹10,000 is deposited and ₹8,000 lent, the secondary deposit is ₹8,000. Credit creation comes from the secondary deposits.
A lower CRR means more credit. With CRR 10%: 100 × 10 = ₹1,000. Commercial banks create credit; the RBI does not.

Reserve Bank of India (RBI): the central bank and head of the banking system, with its headquarters in Mumbai. All banks follow its rules. It issues currency notes, which carry the Governor's signature. One-rupee notes and coins are issued by the Ministry of Finance. It is also banker to the central and state governments.

Commercial banks accept deposits, lend and create credit, and earn profit from interest and fees. Public sector examples are SBI, PNB, BOI, Canara Bank and Bank of Baroda; private sector examples are ICICI, HDFC and Yes Bank.

Cooperative banks are run by cooperative societies under state laws. Rural cooperative banks lend for farming, cattle and fishery. Urban ones lend for self-employment, small industry, durable goods and personal finance. Examples are state cooperative banks, primary agricultural credit societies, urban cooperative banks, land development banks and district central cooperative banks.
Development banks give long-term credit to private and public units to set up industries and infrastructure. Examples are IDBI, IFCI and State Finance Corporations.

vsa: How does a bank create credit?

A bank keeps a fraction of each deposit as cash (CRR) and lends the rest. Each loan creates a new (secondary) deposit, which is again partly lent. Total credit = initial deposit × 1/CRR, e.g. ₹100 × 5 = ₹500 at a CRR of 20%.
What is the meaning of banking?
Banking means accepting deposits of money from the public for lending or investment. The deposits are repayable on demand or otherwise and can be withdrawn by cheque, draft or order.
Distinguish between a bank and banking.

A bank is an institution that accepts deposits and gives loans.
Banking is the activity a bank carries on: accepting deposits for lending or investment, repayable on demand and withdrawable by cheque.

or: How does a bank keep valuables in safe custody?
A bank provides locker facilities in which customers keep jewellery, property documents and other valuables safely, for a rent.

vsa: What credit do development banks provide?
Development banks give long-term credit to private companies and public sector units to set up industries and build infrastructure, e.g. IDBI, IFCI and State Finance Corporations.

or: Distinguish between a lender and a borrower.
The lender gives money as a loan and has the right to claim it back with interest, e.g. a bank. The borrower takes the loan now and promises to repay it later with interest.

vsa: How many types of banks are there in India? Name them.
Four: (1) the Reserve Bank of India, the central bank; (2) commercial banks; (3) cooperative banks; (4) development banks.
sa: An urban unemployed person wants a loan to start a small business. Which bank should they approach and why?

They should approach an urban cooperative bank (or a commercial bank).
Urban cooperative banks give credit for self-employment activities, small-scale industry and personal finance at reasonable terms.
Commercial banks also give loans to start businesses to people able to repay in future.
Explain the working of commercial banks in India.

Commercial banks accept deposits from the public and give loans to individuals and businesses.
They create credit through their lending and earn profit by charging interest and fees for drafts and money transfers.
They are in the public sector (SBI, PNB, Bank of Baroda) or the private sector (ICICI, HDFC, Yes Bank).
Distinguish between a commercial bank and a cooperative bank.

Commercial bank: a company in the public or private sector that aims at profit and serves the general public — SBI, HDFC.
Cooperative bank: run by a cooperative society under state laws for the mutual benefit of members. It gives credit in rural areas (farming, cattle, fishery) and urban areas (self-employment, small industry, consumer durables).
What are development banks? Give examples.

Development banks give long-term credit to private companies and public sector units to set up industries and create infrastructure, which economic development needs.
Examples: Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI), Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI) and State Finance Corporations.
Describe the steps in opening a savings account in a bank.

(1) Visit the bank and ask for an account-opening form.
(2) Fill in the form with name, address and nominee details and attach photographs and proof of identity and address (KYC).
(3) Deposit the minimum initial amount.
(4) The bank opens the account, gives an account number and issues a passbook and cheque book for deposits and withdrawals.
la: How does a bank create credit? Explain with a numerical example.

A bank keeps a fraction of deposits as cash (CRR) and lends the rest; each loan becomes a new deposit.
Example with CRR 20%:
Round 1: A deposits ₹100; the bank keeps ₹20 and lends ₹80.
Round 2: ₹80 is deposited; the bank keeps ₹16 and lends ₹64.
Round 3: ₹64 is deposited; the bank keeps ₹12.80 and lends ₹51.20 … and so on.
Total credit = 100 × 1/20% = ₹500, made up of ₹100 cash reserve and ₹400 loans.
The primary deposit is ₹100; the secondary deposits total ₹400. A lower CRR creates more credit (10% gives ₹1,000).
Explain the primary functions of a bank.

(1) Accepting deposits: the bank opens an account with an account number, adds deposits and deducts withdrawals, pays interest on some deposits, and issues cheque books for withdrawals and payments.
(2) Giving loans: it lends to people who can repay in future — for TVs, refrigerators, cars and houses, or to start a business — and charges interest.
It also keeps valuables such as jewellery and documents safe in lockers.
Write short notes on (a) the Reserve Bank of India and (b) cooperative banks.

(a) RBI: the central bank and head of the banking system, with its headquarters in Mumbai. All banks follow its rules. It issues currency notes (except one-rupee notes and coins, which the Ministry of Finance issues) and acts as banker to the central and state governments.
(b) Cooperative banks: run by cooperative societies under state laws. Rural ones lend for farming, cattle and fishery; urban ones lend for self-employment, small industry, durable goods and personal finance. Examples are state cooperative banks, PACS, urban cooperative banks and land development banks.
